body: The Nintendo DS Lite was announced on January 26, 2006, and showcased at E3 2006 the following May. The system launched in Japan on March 2, 2006. Heavy demand led to widespread shortages, and some retailers raised prices above list price. Nintendo shipped 550,000 units in March 2006, exceeding expectations, yet the console sold out quickly. To address demand, the company shipped an additional 700,000 units in April, but retailers were again sold out by late May. Shortages continued through much of 2006 and 2007.

The Nintendo DS Lite is a redesign of the Nintendo DS. While retaining the original model's core features, it features a slimmer case, a larger stylus, improved battery life, and brighter displays. The top screen has a maximum brightness of 200 cd/m2, while the lower touch screen reaches 190 cd/m2. Its 1000 mAh lithium-ion battery provides approximately 15–19 hours of play after about three hours of charging. The DS Lite uses a different AC adapter from the original Nintendo DS and the Game Boy Advance SP due to a smaller power port on the top of the unit. The included stylus is 1 cm longer and 2 mm thicker than that of the original model.

The Nintendo DS is backward compatible with Game Boy Advance (GBA) cartridges. The smaller Nintendo DS game cards fit into a slot on the top of the system, while Game Boy Advance games fit into a slot on the bottom. The Nintendo DS, like the Game Boy Micro, is not backward compatible with games made for the original Game Boy and Game Boy Color because the required hardware is not included and the console has physical incompatibility with Game Boy and Game Boy Color games.

summary: DS Lite refines the original dual-screen handheld with a slimmer body, brighter displays and a larger stylus, while retaining its DS and Game Boy Advance game libraries.

body: On 2 March 2006, Nintendo launches the DS Lite in Japan. The redesign retains the DS's two screens, touchscreen and game library, but makes the machine more compact and its displays brighter, with adjustable brightness. The change affects the everyday relationship with the console: how much room it takes up, how it feels in the hands, and how clearly colours and details appear under different lighting conditions. Existing DS owners can keep using their games; newcomers find a platform with an established library. That continuity makes the work on the device itself easier to appreciate. DS Lite shows how much an industrial redesign can change the experience without introducing a new generation of games: it makes an object intended to travel with its owner more comfortable and more appealing.

In Nintendo DS Lite, this chapter turns on hardware innovation and physical form. The most recognizable touchpoints are Nintendo DS Lite, but their importance comes from the way they organize attention, timing and choice rather than from name recognition alone. In the context of 2006, the design makes rules and presentation reinforce one another, pushing the experience toward visual direction and graphic identity. Its significance becomes clearer through repetition, when the player stops treating the system as a novelty and starts reading it as part of the work's basic grammar. That is where a technical or structural decision becomes historical evidence: it shapes behavior, produces meaning and creates the bridge to the next part of Nintendo DS Lite's story.

The useful way to read this part of Nintendo DS Lite is through distribution, media and data preservation. Elements such as Nintendo DS, Game Boy Advance, Nintendo DS Lite do not stand apart from the rest of the game; they change what the player watches, prepares for and values from moment to moment. The result is legible because consequences follow from repeated actions, allowing the design to connect systems with design legacy and later influence. In 2006, that connection gave the work a clearer identity than a feature list could explain. Seen today, its value lies less in novelty by itself than in how rhythm, information and decision are arranged into a coherent experience. That arrangement also sets up the article's next question.

Nintendo DS Lite becomes easier to understand when interface, accessibility and comprehension is examined as a working system rather than an isolated feature. Around DS, Nintendo DS Lite, the design links repeated player behavior to cultural impact and collective memory, so mechanics, staging and interpretation pull in the same direction. The key point is not that every element was unprecedented in 2006; it is that the combination creates a recognizable cadence and teaches the player what kinds of decisions matter. Over time, that cadence becomes part of the work's identity and of the way it is remembered. This chapter therefore treats the concrete design detail as a cause with wider consequences, not as a piece of trivia detached from the rest of the article.
